title: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
metaTitle: Got a Mailbox Offer for Your Utah Mineral Rights?
metaDescription: An unsolicited letter offering to buy your Utah minerals doesn't mean you have to accept the first number. Here's how to benchmark a mailbox offer.
heroLead: A letter arriving out of nowhere offering to buy your mineral rights usually means one thing worth paying attention to: someone did their homework and thinks there's real value under your acreage.
intro: Unsolicited offers, sometimes called mailbox offers, show up when a landman or buying company pulls county records, cross-references recent permit or leasing activity, and sends letters to every mineral owner in the affected area. Getting one isn't a scam by itself, and it's not necessarily a bad-faith lowball attempt either — but it also isn't the only number you're going to get, and it's rarely the best one, because the sender's business model depends on a meaningful percentage of recipients simply signing and mailing back the enclosed deed without comparing it to anything.

The single most useful thing you can do with a mailbox offer is treat it as a starting data point rather than a decision. It confirms your minerals are worth someone's attention. It doesn't tell you whether the number is fair, generous, or well below what a competing buyer would pay for the same interest, and there's no way to know that without comparing it to at least one other offer built on the same underlying facts about your acreage.

sections.heading: What the letter usually isn't telling you
paragraphs: Most mailbox offer letters don't explain how the number was calculated, what production or permit data it's based on, or how your specific decimal interest and unit compare to others in the area. That's not necessarily deceptive, but it does mean the number arrives without the context you'd need to judge it. A figure that sounds reasonable in isolation can look very different once you know what nearby wells are actually producing or what recent permits suggest about future activity on your unit.

It's also worth noting that buyers sending bulk mailbox offers are often working with thin margins built on volume, banking on a percentage of recipients not shopping the offer around. That business model doesn't require every individual offer to be unfair, but it does mean there's usually room to get a second opinion before you sign anything.

sections.heading: How to get a real comparison
paragraphs: Before responding to an unsolicited offer, it's worth getting a second number from a buyer who will walk you through how they arrived at it, based on your actual royalty history and current activity on your specific unit rather than a form letter. We'll do exactly that, whether or not you end up selling to us, and there's no obligation created by asking.

If you have the original letter, sending us the offer amount and the description of the interest it references (even without disclosing who sent it) lets us give you a direct comparison quickly. Knowing whether the mailbox offer was in the right range, or well below it, is useful information regardless of what you decide to do next.

sections.heading: Reading the fine print before you sign anything
paragraphs: Some mailbox offers come with an enclosed deed already prepared, ready to sign and notarize, which can create a sense that responding quickly is expected. There's no real urgency on your end — a legitimate buyer's offer should still be available after you've had time to compare it, and if a letter pressures you toward an unusually fast deadline, that's worth treating as a caution flag rather than a reason to move faster.

Also worth checking: whether the offer is for your full mineral interest or only a partial interest, whether it includes any existing royalty interest separately from the mineral rights themselves, and what the effective date is relative to any royalty payments currently in the pipeline. These details affect the real value of what's being offered and aren't always obvious from the letter alone.

faqs.question: Is it normal to get an unsolicited letter offering to buy my minerals?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is a common practice, particularly in areas with recent leasing or permit activity. Buyers pull county records and mail offers broadly. Receiving one is a signal your acreage has drawn attention, not a reason for immediate concern.

faqs.question: Should I just sign and send back the enclosed deed?
faqs.answer: We'd suggest getting a second opinion first. There's no cost or obligation to comparing the offer against what another buyer, working from your actual production and activity data, would offer for the same interest.

faqs.question: Can you tell me if a mailbox offer I received is fair?
faqs.answer: We can give you our own number based on your specific interest, which lets you compare directly. We don't need to know who sent the original letter, just the offer amount and a description of the interest it covers.

faqs.question: Why would a letter push me to respond quickly?
faqs.answer: Some buyers rely on volume and a fast response before an owner has time to compare offers. A legitimate offer should still be reasonably available after you've taken time to check it against another number, so unusual pressure to sign fast is worth treating cautiously.
